results.summary: QTCore-A1 is an accumulator-based 8-bit microarchitecture with a Von Neumann design, featuring a control unit, program counter, instruction register, accumulator, and a 19-byte memory bank. It is programmed and controlled via an external SPI microcontroller using a scan chain to load programs and run them, with the SPI clock driving both the scan chain and the processor. The design requires an external microcontroller with SPI and optionally a button and LEDs for I/O. Notably, all functional Verilog beyond the Tiny Tapeout wrapper was written by GPT-4 through conversation, and the project includes an assembler also generated by GPT-4.

spiPWMio provides a PWM generator on output pin 7 and a PWM reader on input pin 7, with the generator duty cycle set by input pins [6:0] and the reader output reflected on output pins [6:0]. The period is assumed to be 20 ms, and the duty cycle can be adjusted between 1 ms and 2 ms. When the SPI interface is used, its behavior can be configured as described in the specification. The design can be tested by looping back the generated PWM signal to the PWM input pin and verifying the output pins, optionally using an oscilloscope and signal generator.

ChipTune implements an 8-bit Programmable Sound Generator (PSG) that replicates the Audio Processing Unit (APU) of vintage video games, featuring two rectangular pulse generators, a triangle wave generator, and a noise generator. It is controlled via a serial UART interface at 9600 baud, and outputs PWM audio along with square, triangle, and noise signals. The design requires an analog PWM filter and audio driver for testing, and can be interfaced to a computer COM port. Notable for its use of 2x2 tiles and 32% utilization, it provides a retro sound generation platform.

This project implements an 8-bit signed Baugh-Wooley multiplier, designed as part of a third-year neural network project and adapted for restricted IO access. The two input operands are provided through ui_in and uio_in, and the 16-bit product is split across uo_out (lower 8 bits) and uio_out (upper 8 bits). The design supports both positive and negative values using two's complement representation and requires no external hardware. It is tested by applying operands, waiting one clock cycle, and reading the result.

This ASIC implements a CORDIC-locked grid-forming reference and a linear dump-load controller for driving micro-inverters, generating a 60 Hz sine wave via a free-running angle counter and CORDIC rotational block. It produces bi-polar PWM signals for an H-bridge and includes ADC sampling for AC and DC voltages, with error accumulation to control a dump FET. The design requires a complex external system including a grid-tied solar setup, H-bridge, transformer, rectifier, dump FET, and ADC for testing. It is notable for its application in renewable energy control and its use of CORDIC for sine generation.

Solo Squash is a VGA display driver that implements a minimal Pong-like game for one player, where the player controls a paddle to keep a bouncing ball within a playfield. It generates 640x480 VGA output with red, green, and blue signals, along with sync signals, and produces simple tones on a speaker output. The design requires external hardware such as resistors for VGA connection, pushbuttons for controls, and an optional speaker. It also includes an experimental leading zero counter that outputs on the bidirectional IO, and is notable for its educational purpose and simple implementation.

This project is a simple 4-bit current output DAC implemented in analog circuitry. It takes a 4-bit digital input on pins ui[0] to ui[3] to select the output current, which is sunk from the analog pin ua[0]. The design requires an external resistive load connected to the analog output pin for testing. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description of its function.

This project implements a stepper motor controller using a Moore state machine, with a time base to control speed, direction, and step type. It supports full-step, half-step, and double-step modes in both clockwise and counterclockwise directions, with selectable speeds of 1s, 0.5s, 0.25s, and 0.125s per step. The design requires an external clock and switches for control inputs, and outputs to four coils (I1-I4). It was tested on an FPGA Cyclone II, and the documentation includes simulation results and state diagrams.

This project is a simple introduction to Tiny Tapeout, consisting of AND gates that take inputs from ui[0] to ui[7] and produce outputs on uo[0] to uo[3]. The documentation is very sparse, stating only that the author is still figuring out how it works and that it can be tested by flipping dip switches. It requires a 7-segment display as external hardware. The design is notable for being a beginner's experiment with the platform.

This project is a test of the Tiny Tapeout method and system, with no specific functionality described. The documentation is essentially empty, stating only that it is a test and that nothing has been implemented yet. It requires no external hardware. The design is notable only as a placeholder or learning exercise.
